title: Airgapped VPC egress orchestration — Terraform sketch and playbook
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a working sketch for running Redwood Private in airgapped / highly-restricted VPCs where outbound (egress) control, private DNS resolution, and terraform-managed network objects must be orchestrated deterministically. Target audience: infra engineers on private-deployments, SREs supporting customer onprem installs, and solutions engineering preparing deployment bundles.

Goals:
- Ensure deterministic and auditable egress behavior for airgapped clusters (explicit egress gateway or NAT translation points).
- Provide Terraform modules and example usage that encapsulate common patterns (egress gateway, NAT pools, split DNS forwarders, firewall tiers).
- Minimize attack surface and reduce blast radius by narrowing firewall rules and k8s NetworkPolicies.
- Provide upgrade and rollback steps that are safe without requiring remote internet access.

Constraints and assumptions:
- Customer may be fully airgapped (no direct internet) or partially airgapped (restricted proxies only).
- Control plane components (Redwood private control plane) may be reachable via customer-managed outbound proxies or via scheduled bulk sync over an approved egress channel.
- On-prem clusters are K8s (1.26+ assumed), but modules should be cloud-agnostic (GCP/AWS/metal).
- Use of customer KMS/HSM is out of scope for this doc; assume secrets already provisioned.

High-level architecture (summary):
1) Internal DNS tier: cluster pods -> cluster DNS (CoreDNS) -> local forwarders -> private DNS forwarder instances (BIND/unbound) -> on-prem resolver or stub zones.
2) Egress gateway(s): small pool of dedicated nodes (DaemonSet or dedicated NodePool) running egress-proxy (Envoy) + NAT instance. Traffic from app nodes routes to gateway via IPtables or CNI policy.
3) NAT pool(s): short-lived ephemeral SNAT pools, or static assigned public/peered IPs for customers that require IP allow-lists.
4) Firewall tiers: control-plane-only, app-egress, and admin/ops. Firewall rules are Terraform-managed with tags for least privilege.
5) NetworkPolicies: default deny, then explicit allow for known service-to-service flows.

Terraform module sketch (names and responsibilities):
- module/airgap-dns-forwarder: deploys small cluster of unbound or CoreDNS external forwarders, health checks, configmap with stub zones, optional DNS over TLS to internal resolvers.
- module/egress-gateway: provisioning for dedicated egress nodes + Envoy config (L4/L7), certificate references, and an optional NAT instance. Exposes an output: gateway_ips.
- module/nat-pool: manages floating IP objects (cloud) or static SNAT ranges (on-prem via metal controller). Outputs: snat_ranges, allocation_id.
- module/firewall-roles: defines firewall rules for the environment; supports rule-tiering and tagging schema.
- module/networkpolicies: canonical k8s NetworkPolicy templates (namespace-level and pod-selector-based) with allow-lists generated from env inputs.

Recommended Terraform variables and tagging conventions (example):
- var.env (string) -> staging|prod|dev
- var.customer_id (string) -> org code for firewall naming
- var.egress_mode (string) -> none|nat|gateway|proxy; default gateway for airgapped recommended
- tag: redwood:private=true; redwood:env=${var.env}; redwood:role=egress-gateway

DNS specifics (detailed):
- Split-horizon requirement: internal names (model-registry.internal.redwood) must resolve to internal IPs. Public model artifact resolution should be blocked unless routed via the egress pipeline.
- Forwarder config approach: keep a ConfigMap template for unbound/CoreDNS that contains stub zones and conditional forwards. Example entries: forward . 10.1.2.3 10.1.2.4; stub-zone for artifacts.customer.local pointing at 10.10.0.2.
- Negative caching: set short TTLs for dynamic internal endpoints but long TTLs for well-known infra to avoid excessive queries on restricted links.
- Health checks: terraform should register DNS forwarder instances behind the egress gateway load balancer with a basic /healthz check.

Egress gateway patterns and NAT behavior:
- Two operational modes:
  * Gateway-only (L7): Envoy terminates egress requests and forwards to upstream proxies with per-route ACLs and mTLS where available. Best for fine-grained policy and observability.
  * NAT-only (L3): simple SNAT via iptables or cloud NAT for bulk traffic where inspection/proxying is not required. Lower complexity but less telemetry/control.
- For airgapped installations prefer gateway-only for control, but provide NAT pool option for customers that require fixed IPs for vendor allow-lists.
- Sticky source IP concerns: when using multiple egress nodes with SNAT, allocate a small finite pool and prefer session pinning for long-lived connections.

Firewall recommendations (policy examples):
- Tier 0: management plane (ssh/rdp only from ops jump hosts CIDR).
- Tier 1: control plane endpoints (K8s API, etcd, control-plane LB) only allowed from the internal control subnet and redwood control plane CIDR if needed.
- Tier 2: egress gateway application ports (proxy outgoing ports 443, 853 for DoT, 80 if allowed) to upstream proxies or vendor endpoints only.
- Tier 3: pod-egress restrictions (via CNI/networkpolicies) default deny, then explicit egress to egress-gateway IPs/ports.

K8s NetworkPolicy pattern (recommended template):
- Create a namespace annotation: network-policy/redwood-managed=true to mark namespaces managed by terraform/helm templating.
- Default deny ingress+egress for workload namespaces.
- Allow egress to: DNS forwarder clusterIP:53/udp, egress-gateway IPs:443/tcp, metrics collector IPs:9091/tcp.
- Allow ingress only from known service accounts or mesh sidecars (if service mesh used).

Upgrade plan (safe rollout):
1) Prep: create terraform plan in a dry-run workspace; generate a diff for firewall and NAT changes.
2) Create parallel DNS forwarder replicas in a non-production subnet and test forwarding behavior with dig/host tests against stub zones.
3) Bring up egress-gateway in passive mode (accept traffic but route to upstream via a mirror/tee) so telemetry/ACL validation can be observed without breaking flows.
4) Switch small percentage of namespaces (canary) to use new network policy and route egress via gateway (via iptables ENI rules or CNI egress annotation). monitor metrics for 24–48 hours.
5) Gradually promote more namespaces. If failures detected, revert iptables/CNI annotation for the canary namespace and rollback terraform.

Rollback considerations:
- Keep previous NAT pool and firewall rules intact for 48 hours post-migration to allow quick reattachment of floating IPs.
- Terraform state: use locking and keep last-known-state backups. Rollback is terraform apply with previous state file (documented).
- DNS: retain old forwarder config until all pods/namespaces have switched and TTLs expired.

Testing matrix (suggested):
- Connectivity tests: pod->dns forwarder, pod->egress-gw, pod->external-proxy (if reachable), verify ip translation.
- Failure injection: kill one egress-gw, validate failover and SNAT reconvergence.
- Security tests: simulate unauthorized egress (should be blocked by networkpolicy/firewall).
- Observability: verify logs from Envoy (egress) include original pod identity via x-forwarded-for or custom header injected by egress gateway.

Operational runbooks (quick commands):
- Check egress gateway pod logs: kubectl -n infra logs -l app=egress-gw
- Verify iptables redirection (on node): sudo iptables -t nat -L -n | grep REDWOOD_EGRESS
- Test DNS: kubectl run --rm -i --tty debug --image=busybox -- sh -c 'nslookup artifacts.customer.local'
- Force reassign floating IP (cloud example): terraform apply -target=module.nat-pool.allocation

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should the default egress gateway implement per-tenant TLS inspection hooks (privacy implications)?
- Decide on a standard for long vs short TTLs in airgapped environments; propose defaults in module variables.
- Finalize approach for session stickiness across egress gateways (IP vs cookie vs connection table).
- Add explicit support for IPv6 in nat-pool module (currently v4-first).

Appendix: example snippet (pseudo-terraform)
module "egress_gw" {
  source = "git::ssh://github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//egress-gateway"
  env = var.env
  customer_id = var.customer_id
  size = 2
  egress_mode = var.egress_mode
}

resource "kubernetes_config_map" "unbound" {
  metadata { name = "unbound-config" namespace = "infra" }
  data = { "unbound.conf" = file("./templates/unbound.conf.tpl") }
}

Checklist before handoff to SE/customer:
- [ ] Confirm CIDR allow-lists for management and ops jump hosts
- [ ] Validate stub zones and forwarders with customer DNS team
- [ ] Verify NAT pool allocation and floating IP permissions
- [ ] Run canary for 24–48 hours, watch egress-error-rate, latency, and failed DNS lookups
- [ ] Document rollback commands and keep them in customer-runbook

Notes to self (stream-of-consciousness):
- Keep gateway lightweight; heavyweight DPI in airgap invites policy debates.
- Try to avoid long-lived iptables hacks across upgrades; prefer CNI-native egress where possible.
- Coordinate with solutions engineering to add templated customer scripts for troubleshooting (dig/nslookup scripts, iptables snapshot tool).

End of sketch. This doc is intentionally prescriptive but incomplete — will iterate with infra and SE to capture edge cases for metal deployments and strict airgap customers.
